question: Can a state licensing board deny me an occupational license because of a criminal conviction, and how can I challenge the denial?

groups: Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation
negative: employment of persons convicted of barrier crimes

gold_sections.why: The rule: no refusal solely for a prior conviction unless it directly relates to the occupation; no 'good moral character' or 'moral turpitude' terms; nine criteria the board must weigh; fingerprint check at the applicant's cost; written notice of the offenses, the direct relationship and how rehabilitation was weighed when a denial rests on the criminal history record.

Predetermination: a person with a record may ask a DPOR board or the Department in advance whether the record disqualifies him; the written determination is binding; no education or training may be required first.

Applies 54.1-204 to all persons licensed, certified, registered or permitted by the health regulatory boards (Department of Health Professions); the text speaks of licensees, not expressly of applicants.
Example of a board-specific statute that still lists conviction grounds in terms 54.1-204 A disfavors (Board of Nursing: conviction of any felony or any misdemeanor involving moral turpitude).
Anyone aggrieved by an action of DPOR, DHP or their regulatory boards is entitled to review, with appeals under the Administrative Process Act.

Every hearing in a contested case follows the Administrative Process Act; a board member who cannot be impartial must withdraw, and any party may request a member's disqualification by stating the grounds with particularity.
A 'case decision' includes a determination whether a named party complies with requirements for obtaining a license, so a license denial is reviewable under the APA.

Informal fact-finding conference: notice, right to appear in person or with counsel and present facts, argument and proof, notice of contrary information the agency may rely on, prompt decision on a license application, brief written basis for an adverse decision.

Formal hearing (evidence, counsel, rebuttal, cross-examination) where the basic law requires one or the informal conference has not been had or has failed; applicants approach the agency and carry the burden of proof; decisions served with findings and reasons.

Summary case decision: a license applicant may ask for one in writing when no material facts are in dispute, stipulating the facts and waiving other administrative proceedings on those questions of law; the agency must determine within 21 days whether the matter may be decided that way.

Where no hearing officer recommends a finding, the board must decide within 90 days of the informal fact-finding or formal proceeding (or a later agreed date); after written notice that a decision is due, no decision within 30 days is deemed in favor of the named party; the agency must notify the party of its decision within five days.
The final agency case decision is served on the named parties by mail.

Health boards: a special conference committee may deny or grant an application or issue a restricted license; its order becomes final 30 days after service (three more days if mailed) unless a written request for a hearing is received, in which case the board must hold a 2.2-4020 formal hearing and the committee's action is vacated.
A party aggrieved by a case decision has a right to direct court review in the manner provided by the Rules of the Supreme Court of Virginia.
Venue for a 2.2-4026 court action is as specified in subdivision 1 of 8.01-261.
Preferred venue for review of a state administrative decision: the county or city where the aggrieved party resides, regularly conducts affairs or business, or has property affected by the action.

Scope of court review: the challenger must designate and demonstrate an error of law. Facts get substantial-evidence review on the agency record only where a formal record was required (a 2.2-4020 hearing); after an informal-only proceeding the court decides facts from the agency file and asks only whether the result was within the agency's legal authority. Law is reviewed de novo, with due account of official regularity and agency expertise.

Court judgments: dismiss or affirm unless an error of law appears; otherwise set the decision aside and remand; the court may not itself supply action the basic law commits to the board (it does not issue the license).

A person who substantially prevails in the court action may recover reasonable costs and attorney fees (attorney fees capped at $25,000) if the agency's position was not substantially justified, was in violation of law, or was for an improper purpose.
State and local agencies may not require a license applicant to disclose sealed arrests, charges or convictions, and may not deny an application solely for refusing to disclose them.
State and local agencies may not require a license applicant to disclose expunged arrests, charges or convictions, and may not deny an application solely for refusing to disclose them.

nuggets.text: A person may not be refused a license, certificate or registration for a regulated occupation solely because of a prior criminal conviction unless the conviction directly relates to the occupation or profession sought.
nuggets.quote: A person shall not be refused a license, certificate, or registration to practice, pursue, or engage in any regulated occupation or profession solely because of a prior criminal conviction, unless the criminal conviction directly relates to the occupation or profession for which the license, certificate, or registration is sought.

nuggets.text: A regulatory board may not refuse a license using vague or arbitrary terms such as "good moral character" or "moral turpitude".
nuggets.quote: A regulatory board shall not use vague or arbitrary terms, including "good moral character" or "moral turpitude" to refuse a license, certificate, or registration.

nuggets.text: To decide whether a conviction directly relates, the board must consider nine criteria: the nature and seriousness of the crime; its relationship to the purpose of licensing; the opportunity the occupation offers for similar crime; its relationship to the ability, capacity or fitness needed for the job; the extent and nature of past criminal activity; the person's age at the time; the time since the last involvement in crime; conduct and work before and after; and evidence of rehabilitation.
nuggets.quote: In determining whether a criminal conviction directly relates to an occupation or profession, the regulatory board shall consider the following criteria

nuggets.text: One required criterion is evidence of the person's rehabilitation or rehabilitative effort while incarcerated or after release.
nuggets.quote: Evidence of the person's rehabilitation or rehabilitative effort while incarcerated or following release

nuggets.text: If an applicant is denied because of information in the criminal history record, the board must notify the applicant in writing of the specific offenses that contributed, how the criminal history directly relates to the occupation, and how it weighed the rehabilitation factors.
nuggets.quote: the regulatory board shall notify the applicant in writing of the specific offense or offenses that contributed to such denial, how the criminal history directly relates to the occupation pursuant to subsection B, and how the regulatory board weighed the rehabilitation factors in subsection B when making its decision

nuggets.text: A person with a criminal record may ask a DPOR regulatory board, or the Department itself, for a predetermination of whether the record would disqualify him from a particular license, certificate or registration.
nuggets.quote: An individual with a criminal record may request a predetermination from a regulatory board within the Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation or from the Department concerning whether his criminal record would disqualify him

nuggets.text: The written predetermination is binding unless the person's criminal record changes afterward or the person gave false information.
nuggets.quote: Such determination shall be binding unless the individual's criminal record changes after the determination or the individual provides false information.

nuggets.text: Section 54.1-204 also applies to all persons licensed, certified, registered or permitted by the boards in the Department of Health Professions (the text speaks of licensees, not expressly of applicants).
nuggets.quote: The provisions of § 54.1-204 shall apply to all persons who are licensed, certified, registered, or permitted by any of the boards within the Department of Health Professions.

answer:
Only in limited cases. A Virginia regulatory board may not refuse you a license solely because of a prior conviction unless it directly relates to the occupation [N1], nor use vague terms like "good moral character" or "moral turpitude" [N2], though some boards' own statutes still do [N29]. It must weigh nine factors, including seriousness, relation to the job, time elapsed and rehabilitation [N3][N4]. Health-board licensees are covered too [N8]. DPOR or its boards give binding predeterminations of whether your record disqualifies you [N6][N7]. You need not disclose sealed or expunged records [N15][N25], and refusing cannot alone justify denial [N26].

A denial over your record must be explained in writing: the offenses, how they relate, and how rehabilitation was weighed [N5]. Under the Administrative Process Act [N9], you or a lawyer may present facts and argument at an informal conference [N10]. The board must decide within 90 days after it unless you agree to a later date [N11]; then send written notice, and no decision within 30 days counts in your favor [N12]. On a health board, request a formal hearing in writing within 30 days of service of the committee's order or it becomes final [N13]; you carry the burden of proof [N21]. Then bring a court action by the deadline in the Supreme Court Rules [N14], where you live or do business [N20]. You must show an error of law [N16]; a win means remand, not a license [N18], plus possible attorney fees up to $25,000 [N19].

gaps: Predetermination (54.1-204.1) is drawn as an alternative first path ending in a binding determination. A person who gets one then applies through the main path, but the schema cannot rejoin a branch to a step that follows the start without inventing an unsourced step, so that hand-off is not drawn. 54.1-204.1 covers DPOR boards and the Department only (hence its own actor); no comparable predetermination statute was found for the health boards. No licensing authority may require education or training before a predetermination request (54.1-204.1 C).

The fingerprint check is optional for the board ('may require'); the applicant pays the cost of fingerprinting or the records check (no amount in the Code; payment is not drawn as a step), and the Central Criminal Records Exchange reports the state and FBI results to the board or its governmental designee (54.1-204 C). The board must use the state or national criminal history rather than requiring certified court records, but may ask the applicant for more information (54.1-204 D).

The order of review and conference is simplified: the APA requires case decisions to rest on an informal conference unless the party and agency agree to waive it for a formal hearing (2.2-4019 A); the conference includes notice of any contrary information the agency may rely on and a brief written statement of the basis for an adverse decision. For health boards the conference is held by a special conference committee or agency subordinate (54.1-2400 10). Not drawn: the summary case decision route (2.2-4020.1), open to a license applicant when no material facts are disputed; the written request stipulates the facts and waives other administrative proceedings on those questions of law, the agency must determine within 21 days whether the matter may be decided that way, and a denial of the request is not judicially reviewable.

The 90-day and 30-day clocks (2.2-4021 B) apply where no hearing officer is empowered to recommend a finding; where a hearing officer recommends, the agency must decide within 30 days of receiving the recommendation (2.2-4021 C). 'Deemed to be in favor of the named party' is stated by the statute, but the schema's consequence enum has 'deemed-denial' and no deemed-approval value, so the 30-day timer is marked 'unstated' and routes to its own outcome, which carries the explicit quote. The agency must notify the party of its decision within five days (2.2-4021 B); that clock is not drawn as a timer because the Code attaches no consequence and the schema's only non-interrupting option ('directory-only') would assert that the text says missing it has no effect.

The decision table only captures the conviction test of 54.1-204; a board may also deny for non-conviction reasons under its own statutes and regulations. Rule 3 (granted despite a directly related conviction) is implied: the 'unless' clause of 54.1-204 A permits refusal but does not require it. Board-specific statutes still use the terms 54.1-204 A bars: 'good moral character' is a qualification in 54.1-2930 (medicine), 54.1-2709 (dentistry), 54.1-2722 (dental hygiene), 54.1-3312 (pharmacy), 54.1-2205 (soil scientists) and 54.1-2206.1 (wetland delineators), and 54.1-3007 (nursing) lists 'Conviction of any felony or any misdemeanor involving moral turpitude'. The Code does not say how these are reconciled with 54.1-204 A.

A formal hearing (2.2-4020) is drawn as the board's option after an informal decision for DPOR boards (2.2-4020 A 'may'; a board's regulations may give applicants a right to request one). For health boards the applicant's written request within 30 days of service of the committee's order (plus three days if served by mail) makes the hearing mandatory and vacates the committee's action; without a timely request the order becomes final (54.1-2400 10). Whether court review remains open after an applicant lets the order become final without requesting a hearing (exhaustion of remedies) is not stated in the Code. At a formal hearing the applicant may have counsel, present evidence and rebuttal and cross-examine, bears the burden of proof, and receives a decision stating findings and reasons (2.2-4020 C, E). Any party may seek disqualification of a board member who cannot be impartial (54.1-110 B). The formal hearing is drawn as leading to the served final order; a favorable result after the hearing is not drawn separately.

Court review: the challenger must designate and demonstrate an error of law (2.2-4027). If a formal record was required (a 2.2-4020 hearing), facts are reviewed for substantial evidence on the agency record and law de novo; if the board decided after an informal conference only (2.2-4019), the court decides the facts from the agency file, as augmented, and asks only whether the result was within the agency's legal authority. Either way the court takes due account of the presumption of official regularity and the agency's expertise. The court dismisses or affirms, or sets the decision aside and remands; it may not itself supply action the basic law commits to the board (2.2-4029). A person who substantially prevails may recover costs and attorney fees (attorney fees up to $25,000) if the agency's position was not substantially justified, was unlawful or was for an improper purpose (2.2-4030). The agency or the court may postpone the decision's effect pending review (2.2-4028, intermediate relief; not a gold section). Venue follows 2.2-4003 and 8.01-261(1)(a): the county or city where the aggrieved party resides, regularly conducts business, or has affected property. The deadline and form of the notice of appeal and petition are in Rules of Supreme Court Part 2A, not the Code.

54.1-2408.01 literally applies 54.1-204 to persons 'who are licensed, certified, registered, or permitted' by the health boards; the Code does not say expressly that it reaches first-time applicants, though health-board special conference committees do decide applications (54.1-2400 10). Related provisions not drawn: a health licensee convicted of a felony is suspended by the Director without a hearing, and reinstatement requires a hearing and the affirmative vote of three-fourths of the board members at the hearing (54.1-2409); DPOR universal license recognition for out-of-state licensees requires that the individual not have a disqualifying criminal record as determined under 54.1-204 (54.1-205 B 5).
An application that asks about arrests, charges or convictions must tell the applicant that sealed information need not be disclosed (19.2-392.15 F).

notes: Core rule is 54.1-204 (DPOR regulatory boards; extended by 54.1-2408.01 to persons licensed by Department of Health Professions boards - the text speaks of licensees). 'Shall not be refused ... solely because of a prior criminal conviction, unless' it 'directly relates' - so a board may refuse when the conviction directly relates, after weighing the nine B criteria; it may not use 'good moral character' or 'moral turpitude', though several board-specific statutes still do (54.1-2930, 54.1-2709, 54.1-2722, 54.1-3312, 54.1-2205, 54.1-2206.1, 54.1-3007). The written-explanation duty in 54.1-204 C is triggered by a denial 'because of the information appearing in his criminal history record'. Predetermination (54.1-204.1) is binding and limited to DPOR boards and the Department. Challenge: review under the APA (54.1-109; 2.2-4019 informal conference, 2.2-4020 formal hearing, 2.2-4020.1 summary case decision, 2.2-4021 decision clocks and five-day notice, 54.1-2400(10) health-board hearing request, 2.2-4026 court action with venue under 2.2-4003 and 8.01-261(1), 2.2-4027 scope of review on two tracks, 2.2-4029 affirm or set aside and remand, 2.2-4030 costs and attorney fees up to $25,000). Licensing outside Title 54.1 (e.g. private security services under DCJS, 9.1-139; teacher licenses, 22.1-298.1; alcoholic beverage licenses, 4.1-222; motor vehicle dealers, 46.2-1575 'Having been convicted of a felony') is governed by those programs' own statutes, which 54.1-204 does not by its terms reach; 'motor vehicle dealer' was removed from the profile negatives for that reason. Sealed (19.2-392.15 C) and expunged (19.2-392.4 B) records need not be disclosed on a license application, and an application may not be denied solely for refusing to disclose them.
